title: Automate project status updates
description: A system that pulls live task data from your tracker and drafts your recurring status update in the format your team already expects.

pull.title: Pull
pull.content: Downloading the latest changes from GitHub to your computer so your local copy is up to date. Claude pulls before starting work to make sure it's building on the newest version, not an old one.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

slack.title: Slack
slack.content: The team messaging app most companies run on. In Level 2, students connect Slack to their AI tools to trigger workflows from messages, post AI-generated updates to channels, or summarize threads automatically.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

notion.title: Notion
notion.content: An all-in-one workspace for docs, wikis, databases, and project tracking. Used heavily across the AI Builder program as a destination for AI-generated content and as a connected app in Level 2 automations.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

handoff.title: Handoff
handoff.content: When your main agent passes a job to a sub-agent and waits for the result. Cleaner than mixing two agents' contexts in one thread, and the moment to inspect for prompt injection if either agent is reading untrusted input.

read-only.title: Read-only
read-only.content: The first rung of the trust gradient: the agent can see your inbox, calendar, or docs but can't change anything. The default starting state for every new tool connection. Tiny blast radius, fast to ship, and confirms the read side works before you graduate the write side.

automation.title: Automation
automation.content: Having Claude run tasks automatically on a schedule or trigger — without you manually starting them each time. For example, checking your inbox every morning and summarizing it to Slack.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: Status updates rarely reflect what's happening in the tracker. Per [Atlassian's State of Teams 2024](https://www.atlassian.com/blog/state-of-teams-2024) research, 55% of knowledge workers say it's hard to track down information at work despite knowing plenty of people who could help, and a chunk of that friction shows up as status-chasing before the report even gets written.

This system pulls current task status straight from your tracker and drafts the update your team already expects, shipped, at risk, next up. The same research found high-performing teams spend less time on status updates and [handoffs](#tooltip-handoff) and more time on work that moves priorities forward. This build closes that gap by [pulling](#tooltip-pull) the update from live task data instead of a manual compile.

Run it as a weekly paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt), a saved skill, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that posts to [Slack](#tooltip-slack) or email. Every version stays [read-only](#tooltip-read-only) against your tracker.
Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming your tracker, your definition of "at risk," the update format, and who reads it.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that pulls current status straight from my project tracker and drafts my recurring status update instead of me manually compiling it. Ask me questions, one at a time, about which tracker holds the real task data, who reads this update and what they care about, what counts as "at risk," and what format the update has always taken. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview forces you to define "at risk" in concrete terms up front, instead of leaving it to guesswork every cycle.

items: Whether your tracker's status field reflects reality or gets updated inconsistently.
What "at risk" means in concrete terms, days overdue or no update in a set window.
Who reads the update, so the format matches what they care about.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common connectors are your project tracker (Asana, Linear, Jira, [Notion](#tooltip-notion)) and Slack or email for delivery. The paste-in version needs none.

**Create.** Start building the system your scope document describes, and test it on a real export from your tracker. The prompt below is an example of the core task. Your scope document will give you a version shaped to your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Draft a [weekly/biweekly] status update for [project or team name] using live task data from [tracker name].

Context: [Paste your current task export: task name, status, owner, due date, priority. Note the tracker's field names, who reads this update, and the format it has always taken, e.g. "shipped, at risk, next up, blockers."]

Rules:
- Pull the tracker's actual task status, don't infer completion from activity alone.
- Flag anything overdue or with no recent update as "at risk," even if no one has said so.
- Keep tone direct and outcomes-focused. No filler about effort or how busy anyone was.
- Summarize instead of dumping full task detail.
- Output: shipped this period, at risk, next up, one line each with owner.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pulling status from the tracker's own fields means an overdue task can't quietly disappear from the update.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Real task status, at-risk flags backed by dates, a format that matches what your audience reads?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what's off (threshold too loose, tone too soft) and fold each correction into the rules.

items: Connect your tracker through a [tool connector](#tooltip-tool-connectors) and have the update draft itself each cycle.
Chain it to a meeting-notes [automation](#tooltip-automation) so new action items show up next cycle.
Keep a running history so leadership can see the trend over time.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat draft rubric and run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each status update, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, tasks flagged at risk, flags that turned out to be real, false positives, and what rule I changed. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log columns make a pattern of false at-risk flags visible after a few cycles.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Each entry takes a minute. Note the date, which rubric checks passed or failed, and what you changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the system passes the rubric a few cycles straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill, so every run starts from your defaults instead of a blank chat. When the log shows the same check failing again and again, that gap is a candidate for a skill of its own. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write the skill for you, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).
One durable failure mode. Stale tracker data produces a confidently wrong status, a habit problem no automation fixes on its own, so treat the update as a tracker-hygiene check too.
